bsky.app/profile/pwna...

You can go from "high level description of a bug" to "proof of concept exploit" in ~10 minutes.

For folks whose usual modal interaction with LLMs is Google search, online chatbots, or copilot in every microsoft office product, it can be really hard to understand how powerful these models are now. But these scanning everything everywhere is why patching is on an insane cadence right now

That bug at least is patched. But the models can and do happily do that for unpatched ones. A vague high-level description of a bug and a working exploit are not meaningfully different these days. They can be literally minutes apart to a cyber-enabled model!
Another six minutes later
~ 5 minutes later it's found out what the bug is, and what the problem is. Another 6 minutes or so and it's built and tested the core exploit primitive.

Let's ask it and find out

"Here is a description of a bug. Work out the exact bug, when it was introduced, when it was patched. Then develop a proof of concept for the bug that exploits it on a local test"

for a human researcher, that's enough information to get started finding it and then exploiting it. I reckon an expert could track down the details in an hour or so, and maybe have a basic PoC in a day or so, maybe a real exploit in a week, give or take.

But how does a cyber model do?
that story describes a bug in relatively high level terms:

To sort of make the point, let me give an example (that's now public).

Here is a story from today www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/u...

you don't even need the patch! I've seen several times now where someone just alluding to some general properties of the bug is sufficient for the model to hone in on it, find it, and build a working proof of concept, and it can do that in less than an hour
basically: if you can find it with claude, someone else can find it with claude (or more importantly with an abliterated open weight model)

because these are typically bugs that are (a) high severity if exploited and (b) you now have a very much smaller lead over attackers before they find the bug and work out how to exploit it. So you have to patch on an expedited schedule

You don't need the patches to be AI-generated, although many are, for that to cause problems. And some of those problems are happening at a higher rate, but also some of it is happening at the same rate, but under much more compressed timespans, so externally they appear to be much more frequent.

like most security teams, including product security who have to triage bugs, build and create patches, as well as the IT staff who have to deploy those patches, are currently basically all in burn-out from having 3-5x more work than equivalent a year or so ago

worth noting that in many cases this is not AI-coded patches failing, but just AI-found defects happening at such a large velocity that then are being patched and deployed on very accelerated timeframes
